speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, May 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. McDermid that Bill C-13, an Act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Ltd., be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, May 31, I had started the debate on Bill C-13, a Bill to privatize Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Ltd. I had reviewed the privatization program of the Government to date and its successes. Now I would like to carry on where I left off before the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) interrupted with a point of order.
Before I get into the details of the legislation, I want to talk a little bit about process and how we plan to divest ourselves of these two companies.
With Nordion, it is our intention to proceed by way of a third party sale as recommended by our financial advisors. This approach will provide maximum benefits to the existing company in terms of stability of operations, access to new capital, the opening of additional markets through the purchaser, and the synergy of the relationship if the purchaser is in a similar or complementary business.
Subject to the passage of the legislation that we are dealing with today, such a third party sale would take
place through a bidding process into stage. The first round would identify a short list of serious bidders and then a final bidding process. I can see a winning bidder being selected and the deal being finalized shortly thereafter.
I must say in passing that there has been tremendous interest from the Canadian private sector in this company. I am sure that we will see some very active bidding on this company.
Theratronics is smaller and of lesser market value. It is, as a result, an appropriate candidate for an employee buy-out. Because of this we are giving employees priority in submitting a proposal to us. Furthermore, the Government is prepared to assist them in developing such a proposal by providing them with some financial resources to engage their own financial advisors.
I should add that Nordion employees have also expressed an interest in exploring the feasibility of purchasing all or part of their company. The Government has offered them a 5 per cent preference on price for a bid for 100 per cent of Nordion or a 10 per cent discount on shares for a minority interest. The Government has already provided employees with funding to cover the cost of hiring a financial advisor to assist them in evaluating these options.
It is interesting that we hear from time to time that unions oppose the privatization of these companies. However, the employees are very enthusiastic about it and are encouraging the Government to proceed with the privatization because they feel very strongly about these two companies, that they can do very, very well in the private sector.
Let me turn now to the actual provisions of the legislation. The Bill is a relatively simple one, so I do not want to take up too much House time. Clause 4 authorizes the Canadian Development Investment Corporation to sell or otherwise dispose of all of its shares in both Nordion and Theratronics in a manner to be approved by the Governor in Council.

June 2, 1989
Nordion and Theratronics
Clauses 5 and 6 impose certain conditions relating to the shares of Nordion and limit total non-resident ownership to 25 per cent of the aggregate voting shares. Clause 7 restricts amendments to the articles of incorporation that are not consistent with the provisions of this legislation.
Clause 8 provides for a special continuity of employment pension option for Nordion and Theratronics employees. This is a very important point. This pension option has been legislated in all previous privatizations involving employees who were contributors to the public service superannuation plan. The provision allows employees to count the service with the privatized companies toward meeting service thresholds, for example, the early retirement service requirement under the public service superannuation plan.
Since employees of privatized companies cannot contribute to the public service superannuation plan, Clause 9 of the Bill permits the Governor in Council to delete Nordion and Theratronics from Schedule I of the Public Service Superannuation Act.
Finally, Clause 10 deems Nordion to have satisfied the requirements to make its equity an eligible investment for certain institutional investors. This legal for life provision simply facilitates investment by pension fund managers, trusted insurance companies,and Nordion shares should they so desire.
Because Nordion and Theratronics will both continue to serve Canadians and because their location is here in the national capital region, they will be required to provide service to the public in both official languages. This will be accomplished through the purchase and sale agreement for the two companies.
We have also imposed a 25 per cent non-resident ownership limit on the sale of Nordion because we wish to ensure that important Canadian technology remains under Canadian ownership and control now and in the future.
We have elected not to legislate similar restrictions for the sale of Theratronics. We are taking this approach in order to provide employees with the greatest possible flexibility in terms of structuring a proposal and arranging the necessary financing for it. As mentioned earlier,
we are taking a different approach with each company in order to capitalize on their respective strengths.
As always, the concerns of the employees of Nordion and Theratronics stand uppermost in our minds throughout the divestiture process. In order to protect employee interests, the conditions of sale of both companies will require that the current terms and conditions of employment continue in force. In addition, collective bargaining agreements and bargaining agents will not be affected by the sale. The new owners will be required to put in place new pension arrangements that, as a minimum, meet the standards prescribed by the Pension Benefits Standards Act.
They will also be required to enter into a reciprocal pension transfer agreement which gives employees the option to transfer their pension benefits to the new plan. Pension benefits earned to the date of sale will be fully protected and employees will be able to choose from the full range of available options-annuities, return of contributions, continuity of service, and so on-depending upon the age and length of service in deciding how they wish to receive the benefits earned to the date of privatization.
Let me speak to the important issue of health and safety because I know that is an important public concern when dealing with companies involved with nuclear and radiation technologies.
No matter who ultimately owns either Nordion or Theratronics, privatization of these companies will not affect the regulatory environment in which they operate.
They have always been subject not only to Canadian regulations but also to the regulatory environments of the countries in which they do business.
In foreign countries, Nordion, for example, is responsible for setting up the plant, training workers, and ensuring the plant is operating safely before it turns the facility over to the local authorities who then take responsibility for it.
In Canada, regulatory authorities include the Atomic Energy Control Board, which regulates the safe handling and use of radio active products; Transport Canada, which regulates the safe transportation of dangerous goods; and Health and Welfare Canada, whose Bureau of Radiation and Medical Devices regulates medical devices, radiation sources, hazardous products and also
June 2, 1989

enforces manufacturing and product standards. The role of these authorities will continue.
The United States, where there is a sizeable market for Nordion and Theratronics products, has a similar regulatory environment through the United States Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the Food and Drug Administration, and the Department of Transport. At the same time, both companies will still function within regulations established in foreign countries in which they sell their products and under conventions which promote the safe transportation of radioactive materials.
In approaching the divestiture of Nordion and Theratronics, our Government is seeking purchasers who will make a commitment to these companies, a commitment to their employees, and a commitment to the communities in which they operate. We will be reviewing purchase proposals on that basis, because we want these two companies to be stronger and more successful in the future.
I trust that as we debate this legislation all Members of the House from all sides will be looking at the positive contributions that Nordion and Theratronics can make to the economy as Canada as strong private sector corporations.

Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this Bill falls within my area of responsibility as the opposition spokesman for privatization. It is in that context that in a minute or two, I will be saying some things about this Bill.
Before I do that, though, I just wanted to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the two companies we are talking about in this Bill, Theratronics and Nordion, are both situated in Kanata, not far from here, and have implications for that immediate area, including the nearby riding of Renfrew. My good friend and distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Renfrew (Mr. Hopkins), is in his riding today doing what he does so well-keeping in touch with his constituents. He will be speaking later in this debate and at that time, among other things, will talk about some of those local ramifications of the Bill.
I should first take a minute to respond to two or three things that the Minister said a couple of days ago when we began debate on the Bill. I want to thank him for his
Nordion and Theratronics
courtesy in providing me with a copy of his notes as he began speaking on Wednesday.
A couple of days ago, the Minister talked about the Government's commitment in 1984 to revitalize the economy so that economic growth could be strengthened and productive jobs for Canadians created. I do not disagree with him that that is a very laudable objective. It is worded nicely, it reads well, and it tickles the cockles of almost any hearts who are out there looking for jobs.
Of course, it is not 1984; it is now 1989. I say to him that the ultimate test of any of those fairly lofty statements is whether in retrospect the track record indicates they meant anything or whether the Government that melded them at the time took them seriously. I want to give him one example.
I will be the first to admit that with the very specialized products in the area of radiation, chemicals and so on, Nordion and Theratronics are at least a country mile from the fishery off the south coast of Newfoundland. I want, in passing, to demonstrate that the Minister's statement of a couple of days ago in this matter of economic growth and the Government's undertaking in that respect needs a little examination and, by extension, to show the complete relevance of what I want to say here today, to raise the larger question of if his statement on the economy is not exactly what it appears to be on the surface, maybe certain other things in this speech of his bear a little scrutiny as well.
Let us talk for a moment about the fishery, because here was an opportunity for the Government to put its money where its mouth was in 1984 when it said: "a commitment to revitalize the economy so that economic growth could be strengthened and productive jobs for Canadians created". That is a laudable objective. What happened in the fishery? What happened in the 3PS fishing zone off Newfoundland involving the St. Pierre and Miquelon area that Members will be familiar with at least on a map? What happened in the so-called northern cod stock area, the 2J3KL area in terms of the NAFO designations off the east coast of north Newfoundland, the northeast coast of Newfoundland, and the east coast of southern Labrador? What happened in those two instances, the south coast of Newfoundland and the so-called northern cod area?

If we look at the period leading up to and including 1984, at which time we had a Government of another stripe than the present one, in those two cases and in those two areas there was no overfishing. In the first case, there was no overfishing by the French. They stayed within their assigned quotas, quotas assigned to them pursuant to a convention and agreement between Canada and France. They stayed within those quotas every year up to and including 1984.
What happened in the northern cod area? Spain, Portugal, and all the other countries, both NAFO countries and non-NAFO countries, without exception in the years leading up to and including 1984, stayed within their assigned quotas. In some cases they were fishing surplus stock inside the 200-mile limit. In other cases they were just outside, on the nose and tail of the Grand Banks and on the Flemish Cap just to the east of the Banks. In all cases without exception those companies stayed within their quotas.
What happened beginning in 1985? Let me give a couple of figures off the top of my head. In 1985, the quota for France in 3PS was 9,500 metric tons. They took 25,800 metric tons. In 1986, the quota was 9,500 metric tons. They took 26,000 metric tons. What happened in the 2J3KL area?
For example, in 1986 the quota for the European Community, including Spain, Portugal, and other countries, was 19,200 metric tons. They took 110,000 metric tons.
What is the difference? One difference is there has been a change of government, but more than that there has been a change of signal being sent out by the Government of the day to foreign countries. The signal as of 1984 was: "Come, rape our resources, devastate the industry, take the jobs of our fishermen and fish plant workers; do what you want as long as you love us, as long as you are nice to our Prime Minister, and as long as you help him advance his career internationally". The fact that 15,000 or 16,000 fishermen and plant workers on the south coast of Newfoundland see their jobs in jeopardy is a mere detail.
Let us come back to the Minister's statement and to this Bill. It is very relevant, if people outside the Chamber really want to understand the agenda of this
Government, what it is up to with this Bill, and what it is up to generally.
The Government in 1984, as the Minister reminded us, talked about a commitment to revitalize the economy. Where is the proof of the pudding in so far as the fishery of the south coast of Newfoundland is concerned? Where is the economic growth there? How is it manifested in the Government's policy?
I submit to the Minister and the House that the reverse is manifested. What is manifested is a devil may care attitude in terms of the workers and people involved. There is a larger agenda at work which does not take into account the inshore fishermen along the northeast coast of Newfoundland, along the south coast of Newfoundland, and in parts of Nova Scotia, plus the deep sea fishermen, the trawlermen, and the plant workers. In total, 98,800 fishermen and plant workers, in round numbers 100,000 people in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia alone depend on the cod stocks I have just talked about. That is not the total number depending on the fisheries in the Atlantic area. That is just the number who are depending on the cod stocks I have been talking about. There are 100,000 jobs at stake. What is the Government doing? It is fiddling while Rome bums. It is on to another objective altogether. "Jobs for fishermen," it says, "don't bother us with details."
Let me give another example which is probably closer to home in terms of the stated objectives of this Bill. The Bill has to do with privatizing two companies headquartered here in Ontario with some holdings elsewhere including out West, Nordion and Theratronics.
Let us talk about another company in the context of the Minister's statement. He goes on to say in his statement that one of the ways the Government pursued the goal of economic growth was through a major review of Crown corporations. That is an accurate statement. It not only reviewed Crown corporations; it went a step further. In the case of one Crown corporation called Air Canada, it removed completely its public policy objective. Anyone who knows the history of air transportation in this country, the history of railway construction in this country, the history of the Post Office in this country, anyone who knows that the transportation ties and the communication ties have to be east-west to keep this country together.

It was a contradiction in terms from the beginning. If we go back to 1840 or subsequent to 1867 where Newfoundland was trading with the Boston states, where the B.C. coast was trading into the western United States as it is and was then, and when central Canada was also involved in a fair amount of north-south trade relations, the whole concept of a Canada from sea to sea was made plausible by a railway network, by a postal network, and subsequently by some public policy relating to airline transportation. The instrument of that policy in so far as the latter was concerned was Air Canada. That was the reason for it. Canada just did not need another airline to compete with the other existing airlines of the day. Canada needed a particular airline that would ensure that places like Stephenville in my riding, Sydney and Sept-Iles, Quebec which did not have millions of population coming out of their ears, would be able to travel from point a to point b.
That was the whole concept of Air Canada as a public instrument of air transportation policy. That is what is being ripped apart here when the Government not only talks about but rushes forward to privatize Air Canada. Very recently Stephenville, Gander, Sydney and Sept-Iles are four areas that have seen the results in spades of the Government's privatization and airline deregulation policy.
The people in Stephenville and in the entire southwestern part of Newfoundland, the Port aux Basques, the Burgeo area, the Port aux Port Peninsula, the Robinson-Codroy-Valley, are also seeing the results in spades. Abitibi Price, the giant pulp and paper employer in Stephenville, is on the public record as saying that Air Canada will pull out of Stephenville on June 17, a couple of weeks from now. It is going to be devastating to its ability to continue to perform and compete in the national market. This is not a question of moving a few passengers once or twice a year. This is a case in the Stephenville example of a company called Air Canada which could not carry all the passengers three or four months a year. It had to put on a larger aircraft every summer for the last couple of summers. My colleague, the provincial Member Mr. Kevin Allword, the Mayor of Stephenville, a delegation including the Mayor of Gander, and I met them a month or so ago in Montreal.

The best answer of the guys in Montreal who perpetrated this foul scheme was "we were not making enough money in Stephenville with the aircraft. We can put her somewhere else and make more money". I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that the original concept of having Air Canada as an instrument of public airline policy had nothing per se to do with making money. We as taxpayers hope that in the process of providing a service, Government would do so reasonably efficiently. One does not go out and squander money for the sake of squandering it. However, the idea that everything has to make money flies in the face of why we have a Government in the first place. If it is all bottom line and all predicated on how much money we can make, why is the Government involved in anything? Why do we not just give the whole thing over to the private sector? This strikes at the very heart of why we are having problems at this time in the country. We have at the head of the Government that gentleman from Baie Comeau whose complete resume, his whole curriculum vitae, states: "Manager, American branch plant operation-shutdown Schefferville". That is the entire resume.

However, that aside, last November things were going full speed ahead. All we heard about was economic growth and that things were going to be Utopia tomorrow morning about six o'clock. Then, thank goodness for lightning insights, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) discovered the deficit. Suddenly we had a deficit. We did not have it last November, but we sure had it come about April 1.
Now, like closing down military bases, like ignoring the fishery, like socking it to the senior citizens, like the new national sales tax, like the new telephone tax and everything else, the Government has to wrestle this deficit to the ground. But who is doing the wrestling? Who is in there punching out for us? It is the crowd that took over the public debt in 1984 when it was $177 billion. What has the Government done in five years? speechtext:
The poor Minister is in a tender mood this morning. The fact is that the Government's handling of its privatization policy, whatever its objective, has been less than admirable. Part of the reason is that the Minister, who was previously the Minister of Housing and made that brilliant statement about the homeless, is now going to do for privatization what he did for the homeless. That is the threat. This whole policy is being very badly handled.
That is not to say that all the divestitures have not been an absolute boondoggle for the lobby groups. What a happy hunting ground it has been for them.
Let me give an example. Yielding to the admonitions of my good friends opposite, I will talk about the privatization of Terra Nova Telecommunications, a Newfoundland telephone company. That is something I know very well. Until recently, there were two utilities handling telephones in Newfoundland. They were the Newfoundland Telephone Company and Terra Nova Telecommunications, which heretofore had been a federal Government Crown corporation.
Quite recently the Government decided to privatize Terra Nova Telecommunications, which we know as TNT in Newfoundland. The letters have all kinds of connotations in the context of what I will say.
Newfoundland Telephone became the successful bidder and acquired TNT. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that along the way a former Member of this House, a very close friend of the Prime Minister, picked up $900,000 in fees? It had nothing at all to do in terms of affecting the legal transaction, the gentleman concerned is a very competent individual. They were straight lobby fees. He got $500,000 for going after the deal and another $400,000 bonus for landing the deal. Privatization has not been without its benefits for some people, but the people at large-
Mr TVemblay (Rosemont): Not for Canadians?

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
That gentleman is a Canadian. I agree with him, he is a Canadian. I have no argument with that but I say to him that there are a lot of other Canadians who did not quite get $900,000 yet from the Government's privatization deals.
The problem is that the Government has no real master plan for privatization. Today the Government will cure the deficit, tomorrow it will be concerned with efficiency. Every day a new song, every day a new Minister. There is no grand scheme and it is the taxpayers, the people of Canada, who are suffering.
Let us talk about another subject relating to the privatization issue. Of course, Petro-Canada is a Crown corporation, an arm of public policy put in place by the former Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, to ensure that the people of this country through their elected representatives had a window on the oil industry.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Government should own service stations. That is a basic principle of the Liberal Party.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
The public say so. The people of Canada have said very strongly over the past three or four years that if the Government wants to muck around with the oil industry it should address itself to the four majors which are organized from top to bottom, from oil fields all the way to gas stations, not only upstream but downstream, between Imperial, Texaco, Shell and Petro-Canada.
If the Government wants to do something with Petro-Canada and the other three I mentioned, let it divest itself of some of its downstream holdings so they do not have such a grip on the industiy.
I have mentioned how they are looking after lobbyists. They are also looking after the visitors, consultants and lawyers. One thing we can say for a Tory is that a Tory is loyal to his or her friend. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that in April of 1986 the following advisers were put in place working in whole or in part on the privatization of Nordion and Theratronics, those two former AECL subsidiaries, until they were handed over to the other Crown corporation for disposal? This is now 1989.1 am talking about three years ago. We are now finally getting
Nordion and Theratronics
around to privatizing Nordion and Theratronics. For three years this is what we have had working on the deal: three investment dealers, one legal firm advising AECL on the matter, one management firm and one accounting firm. I shall hate to see the bill when the Government starts to privatize Air Canada or CN, for example.
The question I am sure all Hon. Members have been waiting for-particularly my very attentive friends on the government side of the House-is this: Where does the Liberal Party stand on this question of privatization?

Where does the Liberal Party stand? First, we oppose privatization as a means of reducing the deficit. If there are some companies that ought to go to the private sector, then they ought to be considered individually on their merits as to what is in the public interest.

I could have mentioned the fishery and the many people who depend on Air Canada to ship fish fresh out of Stephenville. We reject those privatizations where service reductions will take place, where there are job losses or where there is a poor return on investment for the Canadian dollar. Of course, de Havilland is a case in point. We oppose them in those particular cases. As I said a moment ago, each case has to be considered on its merits.
There are so many other things that could be said about this issue. We are talking about two companies that are relatively small in terms of the over-all context of Crown corporations. Nevertheless, this privatization Bill is a symbol of what the Government is up to.
What is it up to? The sad truth is that it does not have any clear objective of what it is up to, except it has an ongoing right wing policy which will continue to devastate all parts of the country. Apart from that, it is a symbol, a symbol that the Government is completely out of whack, out of touch with the people I mentioned in Stephenville, in southwestern Newfoundland, in Sydney, in those areas where privatization is-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

It is a symbol that the Government and that Minister is out of touch with some of the realities out there. They are out of touch with the fact that privatization, together with airline deregulation, the closing of post offices, rail line abandonments, the jacking up of taxes, and the job losses in the fishery are
causing real havoc with the Canadian people who are not at all excited about the Minister's ideas on privatization.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is probably possible to say more about Nordion and Theratronics in the two or three minutes I have until 11 a.m. than the previous speaker has managed to put into 40 minutes.
This sale has some extremely serious problems associated with it. I will try to go through some of these problems after Question Period. However, I think that there are two points to make at this stage.
The first point is that the Government in its approach to privatization reminds me of a family which decides in the summertime that it makes sense to sell off the furnace because, after all, the furnace is not needed at that point in time. That is the philosophy of the Government. We do not need these companies at this stage. Thus, we will sell them off without looking to the future, without looking to the possibilities which have to be considered over the longer run. Various companies, from these companies to Petro-Canada, to Air Canada, have to be kept for the country's future and for the future of us as a nation.
Second, I am surprised, with the philosophy the Government is following, that we have not seen a more imaginative privatization program. I expect a Bill to be before us almost any day which will set out the privatization of the Parliament Buildings, the Supreme Court and all the public buildings right across the country. This would enable us to sell off everything-one great, grand fire sale. We will then face the future without any of the assets which we as a country have built up over years and years.
It is a silly approach on the part of the Government. It is an approach that it will come to regret. I hope it is an approach with which it will not persist in the future.
I see that it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Conservative Government as part of its right wing agenda introduced legislation to cut massively and to change our unemployment insurance system.
This is the most severe attack on unemployment insurance since its introduction following the great depression of the 1930s. Unemployment insurance was introduced and improved over the years to make sure that Canadian workers have enough money to buy groceries and pay their rent when unemployed against their will.
Under this Bill, Canadian workers will pay more in contributions and get less in coverage. Under this Bill, the Government is cutting its legislative contribution which last year was $2.9 billion.
All this is being done despite the fact that during the last election the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), citing the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), categorically denied that there would be any change or cuts in unemployment insurance. So much for Conservative credibility.
We will oppose these cruel cuts with every means available to us. Hopefully, the Government will start to listen.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay tribute to a woman from Red Deer who contributed very much during her lifetime working tirelessly for the betterment of the people of Red Deer.
Ethel Taylor's political allegiance was to the New Democratic Party, yet she was very popular in traditionally Conservative Red Deer. She was Red Deer's first female city councillor, but she would insist very strongly and very rightly that she was elected for her abilities and her efforts and not for her sex.
I could also imagine Ethel standing beside me insisting that she did not need nor did she want any pious platitudes from a Conservative. She was a person who could work well with others whose political philosophy she did not share. She would work tirelessly to improve services for less advantaged people.
The City of Red Deer has named a street and a bridge in her honour, but her philosophy of caring and sharing and the results of her good work are her most important legacy.

HOMAGE TO CANADIANS OF ITALIAN ORIGIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is the Italian national holiday and I take this opportunity to draw the attention of Members of this House to the important contribution of Italian Canadians to the growth of our country. Canadians of Italian origin were present in our cultural diversity long before we officially recognized multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society. One might say that the first to leave his mark was John Cabot, or rather Giovanni Caboto, who in 1497 left England and reached the Atlantic Coast.
Mr. Speaker, the contribution of Italian Canadians has extended to many areas of our national life and reflects their vitality, their dynamism and their creativity. Canada would not have become what it is today without the invaluable contribution of Italian Canadians. They have understood the true meaning of Canadian-style multiculturalism. They have always been able to reconcile their deep attachment to Italy with their boundless loyalty to their adopted country.
Mr. Speaker, I call on all present here to join with Canadians in thanking the Italian community for the leading role it has played in Canadian life.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND AFFORDABILITY OF STOCK
SUPPLY AND AFFORDABILITY OF STOCK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Housing (Mr. Redway) continues to say mea culpa when he is asked to address the continuing problems of supply and affordability of housing in Canada.
In St. John's this week he told the Co-operative Housing Foundation that "there is little to suggest you should be happy with me."
In Quebec City, the Canadian Association of Housing and Renewal Officials could only wonder why the rental RRAP program was cut from the Budget when a two-year review had suggested no such possibility.
The Minister's notorious "give me a blast" statement over the Government's lack of action on housing only tells Canadians that the Government has failed.
It has failed to provide a minimal 5,000 units of co-operative housing. It has failed our poorest citizens who require low cost shelter on the rental RRAP program. Because of high interest rates, it has failed young Canadian families looking for affordable housing.
How can the Minister believe that admission of failure excuses the shortcomings of his Departments, himself, and his Government? Since when has mea culpa become a substitute for action?

THIRTIETH MEETING IN OTTAWA AND MONTEBELLO
speechtext:
Your Honour will know of several important and valuable parliamentary associations involving countries around the world, but there is perhaps no more immediately fascinating and crucial few days for Canadian Members of Parliament and Senators to spend than in the Canada-United States interparliamentary group.
I am honoured to be a participant in this the thirtieth meeting of this unique organization. Members on all sides of the Chamber plays host this weekend in Ottawa
and Montebello to a distinquished group of American Senators and Congressional representatives.
We will have a lot to talk about informally about an interesting week in both Canadian and American Houses. More important, we will trade views on issues which literally cross party lines and international boundaries: acid rain; the greenhouse effect; transboundary movement of hazardous waste products; east coast fisheries enforcement; bilateral trade issues such as steel; agricultural concerns; energy issues; the future of NATO. The list goes on, as will our very special relationship between Canada and the United States. Welcome, friends.

LINK BETWEEN OTTAWA AND HIGHWAY 401
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent acknowledgement by the Ontario Government of the need for a four-lane link between the Nation's Capital and Highway 401 was good news for Eastern Ontario. What many do not realize is that the Ottawa-Hull area is the second largest centre in Ontario and the fourth largest in Canada.
Since the completion of this new road into and from the capital will be of great interest to the federal Government, it seems appropriate-and it is indeed the hope of all municipalities affected by this initiative-that the federal Government will extend co-operation to the provincial and municipal Governments involved in order that we can see this project started and completed in the not too distant future.

June 2, 1989

citizens in my riding. Everywhere I went, I was struck by the way these people enjoyed getting together and sharing some wonderful times.
The Government of Canada takes great pride in helping senior citizens clubs by supporting them financially through the New Horizons Program. subtopic: PROSECUTION OF JOURNALIST
PROSECUTION OF JOURNALIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision by the RCMP to lay charges against journalist Doug Small sets a dangerous precedent that portends the erosion of fundamental democratic freedom.
Such action calls into question the operation of a free press in a democratic society and the public's right to know what its Government is up to.
The Government's actions are designed to label the issue as a wilful criminal act rather than to accept the consequence of its own sloppy security and subsequent lack of accountability.
At the same time that it casts the blame on the media, the Government conveniently hides behind the robes of the courts claiming it cannot comment for fear of prejudicing judicial proceedings.
The truth is that the conviction of Mr. Small would forever compromise the editorial freedom of every journalist in this country.
The charges by the RCMP involve issues fundamental to our Charter of Rights and Freedoms and jeopardize the concept of freedom of the press so crucial to a democratic society.
This is not a minor matter. The very foundation of a free democratic society is at stake.

CONGRATULATIONS TO KAMLOOPS-HOST TO 1993 CANADA SUMMER GAMES
speechtext:

This announcement was made yesterday by the Hon. Minister of State for Youth and Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Charest) and the Hon. Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Oberle).

MOTION OF STANDING COMMITTEE OF LABOUR, EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration has passed a motion to send a delegation to various Canadian cities in order that Canadians may better exercise their democratic right to speak to drastic changes to the unemployment insurance system.
It is a modest tour of 13 cities, yet it would serve to let the people of Canada give direction to this Government. Incredibly, the Government is preventing a decision of
this important committee from coming before Parliament for approval.
Throughout last year's election campaign, the Progressive Conservatives denied that there would be any changes to this fundamental Canadian institution, so the work of this committee is especially urgent now that they have done an about-face on this important matter.
By this action, whether devious or cowardly, the Government is again denying the people of Canada their legitimate voice on the changes to one of the most significant programs for the protection of Canadians- unemployment insurance.

CELEBRATION OF SENIORS WEEK IN ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next week is Seniors Week in Alberta. Alberta is a leader in offering seniors the support that lets them live their own life with dignity.
Many Albertans refer to Alberta's seniors as our pioneers. This is a society of men and women who see their older fellow citizens as a strong link in our social fabric. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, my question for the Deputy Prime Minister is about the Government's handling of the budget leak fiasco.
Yesterday, June 1, in Hansard the Prime Minister in speaking about what he did the evening of April 26 when he learned about the budget leak said:
I requested immediately that evening that a full Royal Canadian Mounted Police inquiry be launched. Once that inquiry was launched that night there should never have been an attempt by anybody to interfere with the proper conduct of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police inquiry. Everything that was done from that moment on until today has been in keeping with that tradition.
How Canadians can take the words of the Prime Minister at all seriously when we know that the next day after April 26, on April 27 outside the House, the Prime Minister, speaking to reporters and talking about this leak, said: "We are talking about a crime".
How can the words of the Prime Minister be taken seriously when he used that offensive language?

June 2, 1989

The Toronto Star, on April 28, said: "Wednesday's unprecedented leak in Ottawa appears to have been the result of a criminal penetration of budget security". The Financial Post said: "They are considering several potential criminal code violations, including theft, breech of trust, and a possible breech of the rarely used Official Secrets Act". I could go on.
What the Right. Hon. Prime Minister said yesterday was essentially quoting other news sources which suggested the same thing. As he said, he pointed the finger at no one, but there was obviously an illegal, unauthorized release of the Budget prior to the date on which the Budget was to be presented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice. Yesterday I asked the Minister of Justice about an alleged report that his Associate Deputy Minister had phoned the
Attorney General's department in Toronto allegedly on behalf of the Ministry of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, on April 27, the Prime Minister told us-and I would ask the Minister of Justice to go back to Hansard for April 27:
The RCMP is conducting a full investigation. That investigation extends to the actions of presumably all of those involved in that part of it, and also extends to the stock exchanges to ascertain if anybody has profited in any way from any kind of information.

My question is for the Minister of Justice in light of what we now see in Maclean's Magazine. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour as Minister of Veterans Affairs to remind the House, and indeed all Canadians, that next Tuesday, June 6, is the forty-fifth anniversary of one of the greatest days in the history of international freedom. D-Day was also one of the finest days in the history of the Canadian military.
June 2, 1989

All three of our Services were in action on June 6, 1944, the momentus day that spelled the beginning of the end for Elitler and the evil he represented.
Our sailors provided covering fire and manned some of the landing craft. Our airmen helped to keep the skies free of enemy aircraft. More than 15,000 Canadians landed on Normandy beaches to begin the hard fight of delivering millions of Europeans from captivity in their own country.

Mr. Speaker, it will be my privilege to accompany Canadian veterans back to Normandy for this special D-Day anniversary. Together, we will be holding ceremonies at the many memorials and cemeteries that tell of the sacrifice for freedom.

Some 359 Canadians were killed on D-Day and another 715 wounded. Thousands more were killed in the subsequent Normandy campaign.
Next Ibesday let all of us pause in our normal routines and give thought to those Canadians who were called upon to put their lives on the line so that others might be free.
They did us very proud indeed 45 years ago on D-Day. Let us never lose our pride in them.

Mr. Speaker, June 6 indeed marks the day 45 years ago when the greatest assembly of soldiers, sailors, and airmen, attended by equally courageous nurses, doctors, medics, clergy, and many other support groups assailed the beaches of Normandy. They went, Sir, to bring to an end the awful carnage wrought by a maniacal madman. It was the greatest congregation of military might ever assembled. The training, the planning, the awesome courage of these men and women, effected the beginning of the end of Hitler's madness and carnage.

Mr. Speaker, many of those brave soldiers were Canadians, and Canadians they remain. The sacrifices they made so unstintingly, sometimes at the cost of their own life, are the price we have to pay to guarantee and preserve our freedom. I think it is entirely appropriate that this House should take a moment to commemorate and pay tribute to these brave and generous Canadians.

To fail to remember the truly important contribution to democracy of Canadians,to fail to remember them, truly means their ultimate sacrifice was indeed in vain, for in forgetting we condemn ourselves and future generations to its repetition.

June 6, 1944 was indeed an important day for world peace. The majority of Canadians today, especially those bom since World War U, often take our freedoms for granted. That freedom was fought for and it exacted a heavy price. Thousands of our Canadian soldiers died or were injured so that the western world could continue as a democratic society.
The Canadians we are commemorating next Tuesday fought for the principle of peace and for the principle of social justice. Even today our fight for world peace continues as we emerge from the bellicose cold war rhetoric of the nuclear superpowers. The current movement today toward bilateral nuclear disarmament is encouraging and must be continued.
Perhaps the most significant way that we as Canadians can honour our veterans is to in fact honour the cornerstone of freedom for which they fought to preserve. The purpose of their sacrifice was to ensure a world that would remain a free and open society of humankind. We as Canadians are committed to that cause and will continue today through our international efforts hopefully and finally to turn our weapons into ploughshares.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McDermid that Bill C-13, an Act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Ltd., be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start off with some comments of appreciation to the Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDermid) for the quite extraordinary lengths to which he has gone to see to it that critics on the other side of the House were able to receive briefings with respect to these companies, receive detailed financial information, question officials of the company and therefore put ourselves in a position to make comments with respect to the specific companies which are much more pointed and, hopefully, useful as a consequence.
I am going to start off by talking briefly about the whole question of public enterprise in our economy. As the Minister himself noted in his speech, there is a long tradition of public enterprise in this country. He suggested that that was perhaps a tradition on which we should be increasingly turning our backs. My sense is to the contraiy.
It is a tradition which has served this country very well, has given us a railway system which is extensive, profitable and efficient. It has given us the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Radio Canada, which has served us immensely well throughout all of Canada. It has given us in time of war a series of companies initiated by government which met crucial needs for materiel for our armed services during the Second World War. It is a tradition which has given us Air Canada which serves various parts of this country with a sense of duty and a sense of service as something in addition to the concern for private profit. It has given us Petro-Canada which as a corporation has been extremely active in seeing to it that we extend the resources which exist offshore, in the Arctic and in other parts of the country so that we can be more secure with respect to our energy future.
Is this then a tradition from the past which should be abandoned, or is it a tradition which we should build on? For our Party, there is not an ideological answer to that. There is instead a series of considerations which we would use in analyzing the different public enterprises which exist in this country, as to whether they should continue to exist, and also in analyzing the areas in which we do not at this stage have public enterprise serving Canada. Does it make sense to have such companies play a role in that tradition which we have so successfully built up in Canada?
First, it is important to recognize that there are certain activities that the thought processes, the time horizons of the marketplace, do not lead private enterprise to initiate, to undertake within our country, cases of activities which take too long a period of time to mature, for example. There are classic cases like large-scale dams which have pay-offs, but pay-offs which are extended over many years and which the intensely competitive private enterprise sector of our economy cannot afford to wait for returns from.
There are other cases in which the risks in the economic sense are just too high, cases, for instance, in which we are dealing with new and uncertain technologies and where it is very difficult to have a sense of what will happen in the development of those technologies. Often those are areas in which public enterprise makes sense because we can spread the risk over the entire community instead of putting it in the hands of a few private entrepreneurs who are not able to take that kind of risk. Often, too, we may have questions of extreme urgency in which we simply cannot wait for private entrepreneurs to see themselves capable of taking the
June 2, 1989

initiative. That was certainly the case in war-time. It has been the case in other periods of our history.
The second reason why public ownership may make sense in certain circumstances is to give the community a role, a sense of some kind of information, some kind of capacity to help direct what takes place in Canada in circumstances where a small number of very large, often foreign, companies are dominating a key sector of our economy. This was the reason why the New Democratic Party pushed so strongly to have Petro-Canada established. We felt that it was absolutely central to our future as a country that this sector of our economy not continue to be dominated by a very small number of extremely large integrated multinational oil companies.
A third reason which pushes us to look at public enterprise as a response in certain areas is when we are talking about key sectors of our economy in which initiative and innovation is not taking place with the speed and dynamism which is crucial to our future as a country. There, too, it may be necessary to establish public enterprises.
For instance, in the case of the atomic energy area, this was one of the crucial reasons for the establishment of Atomic Energy Canada Limited. This was seen as an area of important innovation. Was it possible to see to it that nuclear power could have peaceful and safe uses within our society? If that was to happen, how was it to happen? Who was to take the lead? Partly because of health and security reasons, we in this country decided that that was an area within which it was important to take a public enterprise initiative.
There are other areas that we as a Party have thought of as areas where public ownership has to be examined. For instance, we have areas that economists often call natural monopolies in which the economics of cost make it important and obvious that one company can serve people at a lower cost than a number of competing companies. For example, two or three telephone companies reproducing a set of telephone lines across the country would not make economic sense. In those areas of natural monopoly it seemed to us to be sensible to
Nordion and Theratronics
look at public enterprise as a way of dealing with this particular economic situation.
Finally, we have looked at public enterprise in provinces where the New Democratic Party has held power. In arguments we have made in the House, we have looked at public enterprise as something that can earn returns and make profits for the people of Canada in order that we will have a return to the social and economic programs which are important to all of us within this country.
With that as a backdrop, let me ask some questions with respect to this particular Bill. What are the issues that emerge as one starts to probe this particular piece of legislation? There are some key process problems to start with. The Minister has brought a Bill before us and in his speech he talked about the importance of satisfying the concerns and aspirations of workers. Yet, we have a situation with both companies in which workers represented by the Public Service Alliance of Canada have been quite concerned with respect to the privatization that is taking place, so much so that workers in both companies voted 95 per cent in favour of strike action during the month of May this year because of their concerns, in part over privatization.

This tells me there are some very important question marks that the Government has not succeeded in settling before bringing this Bill before the House. I must say I regret that. I asked some questions during the briefings which the Minister arranged about whether there were safety questions and whether there were

Nordion and Theratronics
questions with respect to pensions. I was told by the management of the company that there was no problem. Very shortly after I was told that a 95 per cent strike mandate was taken in these companies because of pension problems and safety problems under privatization.

speechtext: Not true.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: I suggest to the Minister that he spend some time talking to representatives of the Public Service Alliance in order to find out whether a 95 per cent strike mandate, which is the vote of workers in the company, does not indicate that there are serious problems with respect to this privatization.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: It has nothing to do with privatization.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
The workers say it is because of the privatization. They voted 95 per cent to strike because of the issues associated with privatization. Frankly, the Minister is going to have to clear this up before he has any hope of getting this Bill through the House on second reading.
It was suggested to us during the briefings arranged by the Minister that these were part of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, but were parts that could be spun off to the private sector because the relationship between these former parts of AECL and AECL itself were relatively unimportant. In fact, when one begins to examine the evidence one finds that these relationships are anything but minor.
In the case of Theratronics, for the most recent full year for which we have statistics, there is interaction with AECL which includes purchases of over $5 million worth of input from AECL. At the same time, Theratronics provides products to Nordion which, in the most recent year for which we have material, amount to almost $8 million.
We also have in the case of Theratronics over $1 million in support for the accelerator products being developed by AECL. In addition, there is a commitment on the part of Theratronics to purchase the key input which is used for this company's production, that is Cobalt-60, from AECL up to the year 2008. We are not talking about arm's length companies, we are talking about companies that have been closely linked in the
past and which are closely linked at the present. That is the case of Theratronics.
Let us look at the case of Nordion. In the case of Nordion those same kinds of connections exist in terms of related party transactions with AECL, and Theratronics providing a lot of input to Nordion and vice versa.
What is perhaps the most serious problem with respect to this Bill in its present form is that there is a commitment within the financial statements of Nordion of almost $17 million. The company itself has assets of about $96 million. With net assets under $100 million, at the same time there is a commitment of $17 million to make in payments to AECL for the next reactor which AECL is setting up for isotope production. Isotopes are the key ingredients which AECL sells to Nordion.
What is most important, and frankly most unfortunate, is that that commitment of $17 million, which has to be put into effect before 1991, is not even included in the financial balance sheet of Nordion as a company. We can see the assets of Nordion, the liabilities and shareholders equity, but there is no mention whatsoever of the fact that this company which the Government of Canada is trying to privatize will have to pay out $17 million over the next two years. There is not one mention of that in the balance sheet of this company.
There is no conclusion that one can come to except that the Government is playing fast and loose with the balance sheets that have been set up for Nordion as a company.
There are also some important information questions which have to be raised. When we talked with the various officials at the briefing, we were told that there is no one in mind at this stage as a purchaser of Nordion. Yet research by The Financial Post, which the Government likes to quote during Question Period, indicates that in its view: "Lavalin Incorporated of Montreal is considered the leading candidate to buy Nordion".
I think the game is fixed. We have a situation where this very profitable company that can give a great deal in returns to the people of Canada is going to be sold to one of those corporations that has been close to the Conservative Party. It is a corporation in which one of the senior cabinet Ministers within this Government previously worked at an executive level. It would appear from what The Financial Post has discovered that that company will
June 2, 1989

be able to purchase Nordion, the more profitable of these two companies.
Those are some of the questions that emerge as specific issues of concern which I think the Government must answer before it can hope to get this Bill through the House at second reading. They are major questions which I think should have been cleared up before reaching the stage at which legislation is presented to the House.
Even if those questions can be cleared up, the basic arguments still remain with reference to the sale of these companies to the private sector.
Both these companies are significantly profitable. This is especially true of Nordion. Nordion has the capacity to give back to the people of Canada some of the tremendous investment which the people of Canada have put into it and have put into the establishment of AECL over the years. If we were to keep this company in the public sector for the next five years, we would get back in profits as much as we are likely to get in the sale of this company to the private sector. Everything after that five years would be gravy, benefits for the people of Canada, which could be taken either in the form of lower taxes or in the form of improved services.
This case, if it leads to the privatization of these two companies, will represent the first time in Canada that part of the nuclear industry goes out from under the control of the public sector. When the Government put out this document about Cobalt-60, it made an important point about AECL, the company of which these two firms have been part. That is to say AECL is the only source allowed in Canada to market Cobalt-60.
Cobalt-60 is something produced in nuclear reactors. It has with it radiation which, as we all know, can affect very seriously the health of people in the country, the health of people working in these firms and the health of other people working in firms in which the products of these firms are used.
This would be the first time in Canadian history in which we took part of the core of the nuclear industry and put it into private hands. What has happened in the United States as a consequence of its nuclear industry in
Nordion and Theratronics
large part being in private hands is something which we would not wish upon our childrens' future.
In the United States it has become more and more difficult to guarantee safety in the core of the nuclear industry because of the short cuts and the cutting of comers which take place on the part of private companies. These are short cuts and cuttings of comers which simply cannot be accepted in a nuclear industry which has so much in the way of risks, so much in the way of security issues attached to it.
It is no surprise when Canadians were asked which of various companies they would like to see put up for sale that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited received the lowest amount of support and the greatest amount of opposition of any company in the country. I make the point that both of these firms that are supposedly not part of AECL are directly, intimately and continuously involved with AECL. They have commitments to help AECL build reactors. They have commitments to buy from AECL. In fact, these firms are part of Atomic Energy of Canada. Yet 50 per cent of the people of Canada in the most recent polling which has been done indicate that they disagree strongly with the sale of AECL to the private sector. They do so because they recognize that there are special health and security issues which come up in the nuclear industry and that both these firms being offered for privatization are part of the core of the nuclear industry.
Finally, I want to make a point with respect to the legislation. In the legislation Nordion is protected from any foreign take-over. We are quite pleased to see that. However, Theratronics, which also has played an important role in our economy, is not protected. There is no protection against a foreign take-over of this important company which Canadian taxpayers have built up over the years.
The last point I want to make, and it is a general one, is that with the Free Tirade Agreement now in place, Crown corporations are one of the few means left to the Canadian Government to take independent action. Under the free trade deal it is possible for Crown corporations to have particular purchase policies, particular investment policies and particular regional development policies without there being any possibility of the United States calling them into question. Yet in this Bill the Government is taking two of these instruments which we

June 2, 1989
Nordion and Theratronics
still have to use, two of these Crown corporations, and suggesting that we strip from our capacity to act in the future these two corporations. It is a serious mistake to do that, especially in light of what the trade deal has brought to the Government and the country in terms of a limiting of policy possibilities.
There are some very specific and pointed problems that mark both these firms to which I want answers and to which our Party wants answers. There are some basic arguments against taking a part of the nuclear industry and putting it into the private sector.
In light of the policy limitations of the Free Trade Agreement, we should keep our Crown corporations, especially when they are as profitable as these two are, so that they can be instruments for us in other areas of policy activity in the future.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the nuclear industry world-wide has been since its inception a combination of a blessing and a curse, of questionable benefits now and in the future. Equally questionable are the dangers inherent in improper use and in the danger of accidents.
People across the country are both attracted and repelled. They are attracted by the benefits provided by nuclear medicine, by nuclear power and by other forms of nuclear research. They are repelled by the very real fears of the accidents that they have seen take place in nuclear power plants in the United States and in the Soviet Union, and more particularly, about the disposal of nuclear waste. They fear that research and development in both the peaceful purposes of nuclear elements and the ongoing improvements to perfect this colossal power will be lost if this power moves out of the hands of a Crown corporation and into the hands of the private sector. To make the nuclear industry acceptable and palatable to the people of Canada, it must be proven that it can be safe and that all humankind will benefit and not be destroyed. With this level of concern among the populace, with this need for close monitoring on the health and safety aspects of the industiy, is this the time to hand over two such crucial components of this industiy to the private sector? No, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that it is not.
We were told in the Speech from the Throne that certain Crown corporations would be privatized when they no longer had a public policy role to play. I fear that the Government is again fooling us with smoke and mirrors. These corporations still have an important role in public policy. From their operations, it would appear that they will have for some time to come. Surely the development of diagnostic and therapeutic materials is a matter of public concern and one that should not be left to the vagaries of the free market system so beloved by the Government.
Nordion, as we know, is a leading international supplier of nuclear-based products serving the world's health care industry. The Industrial Irradiation Division produces half of the world's Cobalt-60 radiation processing equipment and provides 80 per cent of the world's Cobalt-60. The Division's major application for its Cobalt-60 radiation processing equipment is the sterilization of disposal medical and consumer products such as needles, syringes, sutures, bandages and rubber gloves. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that for my constituents and indeed for the people of Nova Scotia, the fact that a company that has a great deal to do with the sterilization of products such as this is one of great public interest when sadly we see this kind of waste washing up on our beaches almost every day.

Mr. Speaker, this is a relatively short Bill with a limited number of clauses and provisions. In fact it does not reflect the care our Government gives each such privatization project. So much so that the Bill is only the tip of the iceberg, as it were, because it deals mainly with the implementation of the process. However there are four more stages, and Hon. Members who were in the House during the previous session when similar legislative measures on Air Canada and Eldorado were adopted are already familiar with our step-by-step approach.
The first stage is the preliminary analysis when the Government considers whether a given Crown corporation should be privatized. That is when the role of the corporation-if any- in achieving public objectives is assessed. Should the decision indicate that public ownership no longer serves the public interest, the Crown corporation under consideration undergoes the second stage, close scrutiny. That examination covers a wide range of factors such as national and regional policy objectives, the corporation's financial situation, the competitive climate, the regulatory framework, the employees' interests, as well as the privatization options best suited to that particular situation.
After evaluating all those considerations and identifying the advantages of various approaches, the Government proceeds to the legislative stage, when sales authorization and conditions to be approved are set out in a Bill introduced in the House of Commons. Members then study the Bill clause by clause and legislative questions are carefully examined. During study of the Eldorado privatization legislation, 67 separate questions were discussed, Mr. Speaker.
Another stage of the privatization process is sales preparation. It almost coincides with approval of the privatization plan by the Cabinet and involves preparing the company for its transfer to the private sector. A team of experts including financial advisers and lawyers works closely with the Crown corporation at this stage.

It allows the Government to see to it that all questions are dealt with in a satisfactory manner and that the interests of all parties involved are protected. The interested parties include not only the corporation and the federal Government but also the Canadian taxpayers, as well as the corporation's employees, clients and suppliers.
If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to describe to this House the way the interests of a very important group have been protected in the privatization process of Nordion and Theratronics. I am thinking about the group without which no organization can survive: the employees.
Nordion and Theratronics are relatively small companies, which does not mean that the Government does not give a high priority to the needs and concerns of their employees. speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS - MOTIONS   MULTICULTURALISM PREAMBLE TO CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, multiculturalism should be recognized as a "fundamental characteristic" of the Canadian nation in the Preamble to the Constitution.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased today to rise to speak on my private Member's motion which states:
That, in the opinion of this House, multiculturalism should be recognized as a "fundamental characteristic" of the Canadian nation in the Preamble to the Constitution.
I expect that Members on both sides of the House and indeed the general public will agree with this motion, because it reflects the reality of modem Canada. Our Constitution, of course, should be based on a Canada that was founded by many different nations of aboriginal peoples whose ancestors today are fighting for their rights amidst a pluralistic modem society. They should

Multiculturalism
also be recognized in the Constitution as our founding people.
Canada recognizes the descendants of French and English-speaking Europeans who settled in Upper and Lower Canada and whose languages today are the official languages of Canada. But there is also a Canada where over one-third of the population, probably more now, has come from none of these origins, settlers from all countries of the world who represent many races and cultures, varied religions and languages and who will soon be a majority group in Canada.
My motion today concerns the official recognition of this latter group of Canadians of many cultures, who have made Canada a mosaic of colour and rich diversity.
Over the centuries Canada has become the home of people from every part of the world. People of every race, coming from many nations, believing in many creeds, have chosen to make a better life for themselves and their families in Canada.
Our history is rich with culture from early settlers. The Maritime provinces, long the home of Acadian populations, welcomed Scottish, Irish, German, New England and Black settlers. The Red River Valley became home to French-speaking voyageurs, English traders, Scottish clergymen, Swiss mercenaries, and the Metis people, the result of inter-marriage with the aboriginal people. The Prairies were opened up by southern and eastern Europeans, who came to Canada with the promise of a better way of life. British Columbia became the destination of immigrants from Asia, many of whom worked and even died to build our railways. Canada, as a whole, has received people from all over the world, people who are interested in preserving their cultural identity as can be witnessed by many active ethnocultural communities across the land.
It was not until 1971, however, that the federal Government recognized the ethnocultural variety within the Canadian nation. Political tokenism recognized ethnocultural groups with fine words but little funding. In 1988, our Multiculturalism Act was passed with strong support from all Parties and from ethnocultural communities.
A parliamentary standing committee on multicultural-ism was promised at that time to monitor this Act. Unfortunately, this promise has yet to be fulfilled in this House. A separate Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship will soon be established under Bill C-18.
Multiculturalism means many things to many people. To New Democrats it is more than an appreciation of different cultures, although our cultural diversity makes us a strong, vibrant, exciting country.
Multiculturalism should promote cross-cultural relations and racial harmony in our schools, our communities and places of work.
The primary goal of multiculturalism in Canada must be to achieve real equality for all Canadians in education, employment and all aspects of Canadian society. There must be equal opportunities for people to immigrate to Canada from all parts of this crowded world with fairer access to people from Third World countries. Immigrants must have adequate language training to settle, seniors must not be forgotten, and women must be protected from double discrimination. Visible minority persons must have equal access to jobs and we must remove systemic discrimination in the workplace with mandatory, not voluntary, employment equity.
Multiculturalism must attack all forms of racism with redress for past wrongs and protections for minorities in the present, and from future discrimination. As an example, the Government promised to acknowledge the injustices of the Chinese Head Tax and Exclusion Act and has not done this. There must be appropriate redress for other ethnic communities that also experienced injustices. We have recommended a redress policy.
Finally, multiculturalism should involve a much more conscious promotion in all of us of a Canadian identity which is greater than the sum of our diverse cultures and which supersedes our own particular heritage.
If multiculturalism is to be more than tokenism, we must acknowledge in our Constitution that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our Canadian nation. Our Constitution lags far behind our legislation and the principles and policies that now are legalized in the Multicultural Act of 1988.

Section 15 of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms is designed to protect minority rights when it states:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
Section 27 of our Charter also recognizes our multicultural heritage. It states:
This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
Many of us thought that this would protect minority rights and preserve the multicultural character of Canada. However we share the growing concern of ethnocultural groups that the provisions of the Charter which I have just quoted may be superseded by Section 33, the "notwithstanding" clause of the Charter, which allows the federal or provincial governments to opt out of these obligations to protect minority rights. I quote Section 33(1) which states:
Parliament or the legislature of a province may expressly declare in an Act of Parliament or the Legislature, as the case may be, that the Act or a provision thereof shall operate notwithstanding a provision included in section 2 or sections 7 to 15 of this Charter.
Provinces or even the federal Government could opt out of the earlier rights. We are concerned about this.
The Meech Lake Constitutional Accord passed by Parliament in 1987, which has not been approved by all provinces, is seriously lacking in the protection of minority rights. The Canadian Ethnocultural Council has stated their position. They would like to see the following amendments to the Meech Lake Accord either as amendments to the Accord or through a companion resolution having the same force as the Accord: "Recognition of multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic alongside such recognition given to linguistic duality; guarantee that the Charter of Rights will not be overridden by the Accord; revoking the "notwithstanding" clause in the Charter of Rights, section 33, so that governments cannot override the rights of citizens when they choose."
The report of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons which was entitled "The 1987 Constitutional Accord" contains our NDP position in a minority report which states:
Multiculturalism
We recommend that serious attention be given to section 33 of the Charter (and that) the First Ministers should discuss its possible repeal in the (next round of Constitutional talks).
The minority report also refers to Canadian ethnocultural reality as follows:
During the hearings, the multicultural associations emphasized the reality that one-third of Canadians are of neither English nor French origin. These Canadians have also made an outstanding contribution to our development as a nation. Today they are an integral part of the Canadian mosaic.
The linguistic duality of Canada has now been recognized in the Accord as "a fundamental characteristic of Canada". The report of the committee states that the ethnocultural diversity of Canada deserves further study. We would go further than this, urging early consideration of the ethnocultural reality of Canada as a fundamental characteristic of our nation.
This, of course, is what this motion does. We would also add the recognition of our founding peoples in any Constitutional amendments.
Modifications to the Charter and a review of the Meech Lake Accord are essential to ensure that the rights of minorities are fully protected, that racism in any form is prohibited, and that the multicultural nature of Canada is promoted and enhanced.
In addition, however, it is important that the nature of Canada's peoples be recognized in the preamble to our Canadian Constitution. This requires reference to aboriginal peoples, reference to the two official language groups, as well as inclusion of persons of other ethnocultural origins. It is essential that our Constitution be modernized to reflect the ethnocultural reality of Canada as a basis for making multicultural policies an integral part of our Canadian culture.
I ask Members of this House and the public at large to support constitutional reforms that reflect the principles in my motion today:
That, in the opinion of this House, multiculturalism should be
recognized as a "fundamental characteristic" of the Canadian nation
in the Preamble to the Constitution.
