In fact, during the constitutional talks in 1980, and the Hon. Member is certainly more experienced in this area than I am, because I was elected in 1984, while she was elected well before then, at the time, the intention had been to enshrine in the preamble the great common values shared by all Canadians.
Unfortunately, at the time, govemements failed to agree on the wording of such a preamble or on any other item on the agenda.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to tell you about a personal experience. In 1978, before I entered politics, I had been appointed General Director of a School Board. At the time, people were starting to talk about- In Quebec, Mr. Morin had published a book which insisted that the school system should be used as a vehicle for teaching values. Meetings were hurriedly organized and we suddenly discovered that our program of studies were pushing no values. We started working in earnest. When the lobbyists who had pushed for schools with values came to see us, we asked them to suggest something.
June 2, 1989

So we took the "something" they had proposed and we tried to improve on it by consulting people. We started by saying: The first value we should develop in education is quality teaching. That was great! So we started to work on this, so once you have a value, you have to define it. We tried to describe what we felt was quality education. So far so good. But there was another group of lobbyists who said: It is very nice to have quality education, but we should rather say religious quality education. That was another problem. That is when the trouble started. We said: That is fine, but what religion? A quality language education. But what language?
When people start defining things-because while one group was working on quality education, another group was working on religion. Still another group was working on language.
Then, because they did not want to be left behind, the teachers of physical education said: It is all very nice to have quality religious education, quality language teaching, why not also quality physical education? We were stuck and we have been stuck for the past eleven years because we wanted to include all the subjects and all the programs in our definitions. That is where the problem often arises. That is what happened in 1980. When we want to name values, when we want to name multicultural groups, when we want to start defining them, we very often forget some and we leave important items out of this definition. Discussions have been going on for 11 years. Three or four Ministers started to say that we really should define it in a "directive" way, but no one has dared to do so yet.
So after the attempt at unilateral repatriation, the Government of Canada and nine provinces agreed on the 1982 Constitution Act. Nevertheless, when we look at that Act, we see nothing about the nature of the society for which it is the fundamental law. There is no preamble, except in the Charter of Rights which recognizes the supremacy of God and the rule of law. That is the only preamble there is in the law. But the inability to agree on a preamble in 1982 does not mean that nothing has been done to define our basic values. It might be said that instead of starting with a preamble identifying these values, Canadians preferred to proceed in stages, and that is where Bill C-73 came in. In 1982, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms was enshrined and is now a fundamental value shared by all Canadians. The Constitution has also recognized the rights of Canada's
Multiculturalism
native peoples. The objective of promoting and maintaining the multicultural heritage of Canadians was also affirmed in 1982.
The Constitution also recognizes the importance of regional vitality in Canada by committing Parliament and the Government of Canada to respecting the principle of equalization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak today in the House to the motion presented by the Member from Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). The question that we must address is whether the House should recognize multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian nation in the preamble to our Constitution.
Canada is a diverse nation with people from around the world choosing it as their adoptive home. We have become recognized globally as a nation that cares about the underprivileged and the troubled. Canada has opened its doors to the world. As a result of the various waves of immigration that have flocked to this country, its face has been permanently changed. At first Canada was home to a diverse array of people who had crossed into North America many thousands of years ago. Aboriginal Canadians have shaped Canada's history and heritage since before the arrival of Jacques Cartier, Champlain or even the Norse that established temporary fishing communities on the shores of Newfoundland.

The following wave of immigration to Canada saw the establishment of French colonies on the East Coast, mainly in Louisbourg, Nova Scotia, in Quebec City and in Hochelaga. They were valiant immigrants who laid the foundations of Canada's French heritage. They were the fathers of French Canadian society, which can be found

June 2, 1989
Multiculturalism
today in all regions of our country. These immigrants worked the land, hunted and fished, in circumstances made difficult by Canada's climate and geography. They laid the foundation on which those who came later would develop and contribute to this country. As part of one of the founding nations of North America, the French pioneers gave Canada its own identity which is unique in the world.
The people of the British Isles provided Canada with its other linguistic dimension. Communities in the Mari-times, Upper Canada, and post-conquest Quebec proved to be of ultimate importance to the evolution of Canada. The British gave this country its political heritage. After all, the institutions of Parliament and the allegiance to the Crown have been given to Canada by its British ancestry.
One cannot separate multiculturalism from the history of Canada. From the outset, we were a country of many different people.
When Canada entered this new century, its characteristics began to change quickly. In addition to the thousands of Chinese who immigrated to Canada to help us complete the CP Railway, there were vast immigrations of Ukrainians, Germans, and Poles. These people were instrumental in settling the western provinces and providing them with a distinct cultural and linguistic heritage.
The arrival of Jewish immigrants from Russia also proved to be an important element in the history of major centres such as Montreal, Vancouver, and Winnipeg. Those people proved to be the lucky ones in that they managed to escape the atrocities of Europe in the 1930s and 1940s.
Canada has opened its arms to those people, and they have had a profound impact on how we view ourselves and how the world looks at us. The potential is there for Canada to be an even better example to the world. We can show that all peoples of all backgrounds can live together in peace and prosperity. It is clear that Canada's
multicultural heritage is an instrumental part of the Canadian experience.
It is for this reason that I feel the motion is worthwhile. The constitution of a country is supposed to reflect the fundamental principles upon which it is built. It is supposed to be representative of the people who live in the country. The entrenchment of multiculturalism in the preamble of the Constitution is obviously in the spirit of the document.
There are several problems with the motion presented by the Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). First, it is not clear where the Hon. Member would like to see the Constitution amended. As far as I can see, it would be inappropriate in the Constitution Act of 1982, or the BNA Act of 1867. In fact, the only place that this would be appropriate would be in amending Section 2 of the Meech Lake Accord to include our multicultural heritage as a fundamental characteristic of Canada. If that is the case then the motion as presented by the Hon. Member would make more sense. In fact, this is the exact position that members of the Liberal Party have taken all along. It was on our list of proposed amendments that we introduced when Meech Lake was before the House of Commons in 1987.
I believe that the Hon. Member for Vancouver East feels that the House should nevertheless adopt this motion because of the positive signal it sends to Canada's ethnic communities, and for this reason I feel it is a productive move. However, I feel as Canadians concerned with the preservation and promotion of our ethnic diversity, we should be concentrating our efforts in other areas.
We should concentrate on promoting greater understanding among ethnic groups in Canada, as well as facilitating the transition of new Canadians into productive and participating citizens. Although the amendment to the preamble of Meech Lake would prove to be a positive symbolic step, it would do little in terms of concrete improvement of ethnic Canadians' standing within our society.
We must work toward the elimination of discrimination in employment practices through a strengthening of the Employment Equity Act. We can achieve greater ethnic harmony through a review of government policy, and through a more effective educational program that will facilitate this end.
June 2, 1989

Section 27 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, an historic achievement of the previous Liberal Government, states quite clearly:
This Charier shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
I cannot think of any clearer way of articulating multiculturalism in the Constitution than has already been done by former Prime Minister Trudeau.
In July of last year our Party position was to strengthen this aspect, along with the entire Charter, by eliminating the notwithstanding clause of the Constitution. Through such an action, which I am afraid to say the Government has too small a backbone to do, Section 27 would be greatly enhanced and multiculturalism would become an unimpeded element of the Canadian Constitution.
In conclusion, I would like to say that this motion, although not terribly original, is a move that I feel the entire House can and should adopt. The entrenchment of multiculturalism in our Constitution is a gesture that should be welcomed by Members on all sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to rise and to this motion No. 293 introduced by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell).
What is a nation? What are the aspects that constitute a nation? According to Webster's Dictionary, it is a geography, a physical entity in any part of the world where not only cultural but social, economic and political aspects are considered in that given locality.
It is in this context as we speak today of the Canadian nation, that this Private Member's motion strives to include multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of our nation, that I rise with great pleasure.
The Canadian nation is about the Canadian people, those indigenous in the country, bom here originally, and those who came after, the immigrants-those of French origin, those of English, Ukrainian, Polish, Jewish, Filipino, Indian origin and others. The Canadian nation is bonded together by the sinews of our diversity.
The character of a nation is and ought to be recognized in its fundamental document, its constitution. We have
June 2, 1989

to recognize that all members of our Canadian society have equal rights and equal responsibilities.
The Meech Lake Accord failed to include an amendment from the Liberal Party that multiculturalism be recognized as a distinct feature of our Canadian society. Since the preamble of any constitution in essence can be considered its soul, the multicultural distinctness of our country has to be included and enshrined in this document multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of our Constitution to reassure the eight million Canadians of non-aboriginal, non-francophone, non-anglophone origins that they too are truly part of our great Canadian nation. This is important because multiculturalism is about human dignity. That an individual is honoured, respected, treated and even asked to serve irrespective of race, colour, creed and any physical characteristic.
Multiculturalism is about tolerance, that others not only should allow everyone to pursue his or her own individual aspirations, it should be allowed to be pursued notwithstanding differences in appearance, accent and traditions.
Multiculturalism is about employment equity. It is about affirmative action programs. Affirmative action programs are based on the principle that merit is the basis for employment, irrespective of colour, creed and physical characteristics. Regrettably, today we still see bases of inequities in the Public Service.
The Public Service Employment Act still gives preference to Canadian citizens and not quite equally to landed Canadian immigrants. I submit that immigration is the beginning of citizenship and the privileges of employment should be given to the landed immigrants equally with Canadian citizens.
Multiculturalism is also about equal access to affordable housing and it is also about human rights. Therefore, it was a great disappointment when the Government, despite its proclamation that it is committed to multiculturalism, saw fit in the Budget to reduce the budgetary allocation for multiculturalism. I had hoped that the Government would have introduced a Budget that would allow the growth and strengthening of multiculturalism.
Hence, this Private Member's motion by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East is a signal to us that yes, we
Multiculturalism
must work together as a unified House so that we may promote social harmony, for we are all Canadians in a great Canadian nation. I salute and thank the Hon. Member for Vancouver East in introducing this motion.

Multiculturalism, Mr. Speaker, for the Hon. Member's information, is a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society. It is in Quebec as well as in Ontario or British Columbia. Last year, for instance, this House unanimously approved the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, thereby emphasizing that multiculturalism per se is a fundamental characteristic of our society. That Act recognizes the pluralistic nature of our society and points to this Government's commitment to ensure the conti-bution and participation of every Canadian.

Multiculturalism
Wherever you go, whether it is Montreal, Vancouver or Winnipeg, you will find concrete signs of the importance of muticulturalism in our society. Canada was not built in a day. Our realities are not carved in stone; rather, Canada is a society forever growing! It grew with each new generation, each new wave of immigrants that came here to find a new kind of freedom. It grew because of the experience, customs and values they contributed. It grew, learned and developed socially and economically because it is an open society.
Mr. Speaker, this is what we should and will continue to do if our society is to improve. In my own province of Quebec, some people don't quite understand the advantages of a multicultural society and refuse to contemplate, accept and enjoy those advantages. Canadian society is not perfect. It is not immune to prejudice and discrimination. It is questioned by all those who, throughout Canada, would like to go back in time.
Mr. Speaker, some people consider diversity a weakness rather than a strength. They believe that, to be a true Canadian, you must assimilate. They feel threatened by our modem pluralistic society.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind you and all other members in this House that if that attitude had prevailed in the past, the Canada we know would not exist today. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the principles entrenched in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, including the principle that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our society, are among those which have sustained Quebec and allowed it to preserve its uniqueness.
Mr. Speaker, the values and principles underlying the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, the notion that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of our society, are some of the traits that distinguish Canada from its American neighbour. I cannot see how Canada could survive in an American ocean without the vibrant dimension which French Canada gives it. It is French Canada, it is the fact that we, as Canadians, have built a bilingual and multicultural society, that fundamentally distinguishes our country from the United States. I cannot imagine Canada not respecting its multicultural diversity-
Mr. Speaker, getting back to the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) I say to her, as a Quebecer: Let us first finalize the Meech Lake Accord, and then we can consider the next series of constitutional changes. Her motion, although well meaning, is inappropriate. We should undertake now to bring the federal family together and Quebec back into the fold as a proud and full-fledged partner. Let us now ratify the Meech Lake Accord!
Mr. Speaker, this is the message I should like to convey to the Hon. Member, for we have an opportunity, with the Meech Lake Accord, to work together and build a Constitution made-in-Canada which truly reflects our identity.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) as well as her Liberal provincial colleagues in Manitoba and New Brunswick not to delay dally any longer, and stop opposing the century old dream of Canadians for a unique Constitution based on participation. With the full and enthusiastic participation of Quebec, we could all get together and create a complete constitutional framework which would reflect the best elements of our Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on the motion of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). I come from a small town in Saskatchewan called Domremy, the namesake of the place where Joan of Arc was born in France. The basic population of the community is French. Some of my neighbours were the original people of Canada.
My parents came from Norway as children and later became Canadian citizens. The type of communities in which we live in western Canada are already multicultural communities. In Canada we decided not to become a melting pot like the nation to the south of us decided to become, but to recognize the differences of the people when they came to Canada as well as the culture of their original nations.
Saskatchewan is the only province in Canada where more than 50 per cent of the population is neither French nor English. In other words, as the Hon. Member from Edmonton pointed out, every group in Saskatche-
June 2, 1989

wan is a minority. We decided to become a mosaic rather than a melting pot.
I want to deal for a moment or two with the history of multiculturalism in western Canada. We went through a period of a great deal of friction, a great deal of confrontation between specific cultural groups. We solved that problem, sometimes with a great deal of difficulty. This gave us an acceptance of multiculturalism. Most of the immigrants who came to the West settled into communities and spoke their original language for a good portion of the time. If one travels to Saskatchewan now, one will see that in the West there are still communities in which the people speak German, Norwegian, French or Italian.
We made the adjustment. It was somewhat difficult for western Canada when suddenly one of those groups became more equal than the rest of the groups. It received a great deal of assistance for its culture. We must recognize that culture is very closely related to language. The people of that group received a lot more assistance for their culture as a result of the bilingualism decision taken by the Government of the day.
Western Canadians recognize the founding structure of Canada. They recognize that this was a good reason for having a bilingual country, and a good reason for leaving it that way. However, they do not have and did not have the protection or the recognition that they needed. There was a great movement when the Constitution was brought before the country in 1982 to make it a multicultural Constitution. That Constitution was accepted and we have a recognition of multiculturalism there. I agree with my colleague for Vancouver East, that it would strengthen the position of multiculturalism in Canada if we recognized it in the preamble of the Constitution. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS - MOTIONS   MULTICULTURALISM PREAMBLE TO CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to participate in this afternoon's debate, to consider the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East, to the effect that the phrase, and I quote: "multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society", be included in the Constitution of the country.
I know that I am joined by every Member in this Chamber, when I say that all of us recognize that Canada is a land built by the contributions of people from all comers of the globe. Indeed, the noted economist Barbara Ward has said that Canada is the first international nation.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, last year this Parliament unanimously approved the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. That legislation was led through this Chamber by the Hon. Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship, the Member for Pierrefonds-Dollard (Mr. Weiner).
Unanimous approval is not something which we give in this place very often. That it was given in this case shows to me the extent to which Members from both sides in this House, and indeed Members from both sides in the other House, came together to recognize the importance of the parliamentary statements that are contained in that historic piece of legislation.
I would also like to take a moment to remind this House of the co-operative and conciliatory way in which the Canadian Multiculturalism Act was passed through this Chamber. The record is clear, the Government sought to develop and nuture a consensus, and it listened as it promised it would. It made changes to make the Act the best possible one, as it promised it would.

Multiculturalism
In considering this debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East, it is instructive to examine carefully the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, its Preamble, and its historic Section 3 which embodies the world's first national legislated multiculturalism policy, a policy which is light years in advance of that merely administrative instrument that the previous Liberal Government introduced in 1971, and did not change for some 14 years.
What strikes me about the Canadian Multiculturalism Act that we here in Parliament affirmed was the importance of multiculturalism in our society. We affirmed that our recognition of multiculturalism was founded, indeed rooted, in our constitutional framework, in the Statutes of Parliament and in several international conventions and instruments. I found at the end of the Preamble of the Canadian Multiculturalism Act a very ringing affirmation of how this House feels about multiculturalism. I think that we would all share this today. I would like to take a moment to read it if I may.
The last clause reads:
And, whereas the Government of Canada recognizes the diversity of Canadians as regards race, national or ethnic origin, colour and religion as a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society, and is committed to a policy of multiculturalism designed to preserve and enhance the multicultural heritage of Canadians while working to achieve the equality of all Canadians in the economic, social, cultural and political life of Canada.
These are very moving words. Members may be aware that they came, interestingly enough, from an amendment brought to this place by the then Member for Thunder Bay, Mr. Epp, on behalf of the New Democratic Party and accepted without change by the Government. I want to emphasize those words "a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society."
I would further want to turn to Section 3 of the Canadian Multiculturalism Act. Section 3.1(b) reads:
It is hereby declared to be the policy of the Government of Canada to recognize and promote the understanding that multiculturalism is a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian heritage and identity, and that it provides an invaluable resource for shaping Canada's future.
You are indicating that we have time problem, Mr. Speaker.
Parliament has spoken. Multiculturalism has been recognized by Parliament to be a fundamental characteristic of Canadian society. All Members who were here made that affirmation together.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I just want to get to the heart of the matter. The motion by the Hon. Member from Vancouver East is about amending our Constitution. It is a motion about the next phase of the evolution of the Canadian Constitution. I think surely that Meech Lake has to come first.
